title: Resources
text:
The instruments below were developed over three years by working groups within the Across the PONs collaborative and are openly available on the Open Science Framework. They are free to use.
Our aim in developing them is simple. If enough scholars collect data on purpose-oriented networks using common measures, the field gains a comparative evidence base no single individual could build. Translations of the instruments and codebooks into Spanish and Dutch are in progress. With other languages planned.
Instruments exist in parallel versions for the two policy domains, human services and environmental governance, since some measures require domain-specific wording.


A semi-structured interview guide for the network manager or convener, covering the history of and motivation for the network, the environment it operates in, its primary activities and theory of change, and how it is managed. This is typically the entry point into a network, conducted before either survey. The guide applies across policy domains, so a single version serves both human services and environmental networks.

A short survey of the network’s leadership team, capturing mandate details, resource munificence, and governance arrangements.

title: Resources
text:
Using the Instruments
Scholars are welcome to deploy these instruments in their own research. The collaborative operates under a data-use and sharing agreement that allows new members to join and contribute cases to the shared database.
If you plan to use an instrument, or are interested in contributing data, please contact members of the coordinating committee:
Michael D. Siciliano, Jörg Raab, Michelle Shumate, and Robin LeMaire.
We can provide access to a Qualtrics version of the survey along with a guide on how to launch it with your particular PON.

title: Resources
text:
Working Papers
Alongside the instruments, the Across the PON’s working groups have produced a series of papers taking stock of the field and setting out directions for future research.

How the Forest Shapes the Trees: Context Mechanisms and Purpose-Oriented Networks
Context is usually treated as a static backdrop in PON research. This paper argues instead that context is an active force that permeates network boundaries and conditions their trajectories, and develops a framework identifying three classes of contextual mechanism — norms, resources, and historical dynamics — operating across five nested layers from the supranational to the community.
Albrecht, K., Raab, J., Sánchez, J., Nowell, B., Kapucu, N., Milward, H. B., & Shumate, M. (April 2026). Read on SSRN


Linking Inputs to Network Dimensions in Purpose-Oriented Networks
Research on PONs has largely treated network structure as a predictor of effectiveness. This paper reverses that direction, asking what gives rise to different relational patterns in the first place, and links five inputs — purpose, organizational capacity, resource munificence, degree of mandate, and external stability — to network structure, composition, and dynamics.
Medina, A., Siciliano, M., Hu, Q., Morçöl, G., & Whetsell, T. (April 2026). Read on SSRN


From Modes to Myths: Untangling Governance, Management, and Institutional Elements in the Modes of Network Governance Typology
Provan and Kenis’s governance mode typology remains the dominant framework for analyzing how PONs are governed, yet what counts as governance — and how it differs from network management — remains persistently ambiguous. Drawing on an institutional perspective, this paper separates governance as constitutional and collective-choice rules from management as operational process, and argues for more rigorous justification of how governance modes are classified.
Sánchez, J., Lemaire, R., Mannak, R., Medina, A., van den Oord, S., Kenis, P., Kapucu, N., Milward, H. B., & Raab, J. (December 2025). Read on SSRN

title: Across the PONs
text:
Public problems rarely respect organizational and jurisdictional boundaries. The collaborative arrangements that form around them, known as purpose-oriented networks (PONs), have become a central instrument of governance, yet we know remarkably little about how their structure and performance vary across national contexts.
Across the PONs is a group of international scholars interested in examining purpose-oriented networks in different national contexts. Where existing research draws overwhelmingly on single-country evidence and single case studies, this project takes a team science approach to build a one-of-a-kind database of PONs. We have developed common survey instruments and interview guides to allow for comparative research across contexts.
Our work combines comparative case analysis with social network analysis to ask what national institutional context does to collaborative governance.
Our hope is that other scholars will join this effort, use our data collection instruments, and contribute to growing a database and repository of knowledge on PONs.

title: About the Project
text:
Communities everywhere face problems no single organization can solve such as pandemics, homelessness, flooding, and wildfires. Responses to these complex issues tend to be in the form of a coordinated arrangement across levels of government and sectors. Purpose-oriented networks, or PONs, are the formalized version of that response. PONs are defined as three or more organizations that consciously affiliate around a shared purpose.
PONs are everywhere in practice, and they have been studied for decades. But as typically studied, scholars tend to focus on a single network in a single context. In part, because gaining access to PONs can be difficult and collecting network data is time consuming.
We see the field as having a shortage of comparable data. Testing whether a proposed relationship holds requires many networks, observed over time, measured the same way. That is data no single scholar and no single lab can assemble. It was this data challenge that gave rise to Across the PONs.

title: About the Project
text:
How the collaborative came together

2022 — Barcelona. A small group of network scholars gathered at ESADE, just emerging from COVID and meeting in person for the first time in over two years. The question on the table was where purpose-oriented network research was headed and what was missing. The proposal made there was a team science one: if enough of us collected data on a few networks each, using a shared instrument, we could build collectively what none of us could build alone. Across the PONs began at that meeting.
2023 — Tilburg. The group assembled a wish list of hypotheses we would test given data on hundreds of networks at multiple points in time, all measured the same way. That list was translated into specific variables and organized into four thematic working groups: context, structure and inputs, governance, and process and outputs. Each group spent the following year determining exactly what to measure and how.
2024 — Chicago. The working groups reconvened to combine their measures and draft the instruments themselves.
Now. Three instruments exist — an interview guide for network managers, a survey for network leaders, and a survey for organizational members — along with their codebooks. They are openly available on the Open Science Framework. The first wave of data collection using these instruments is underway.

The collaborative now includes scholars across the globe, ranging from doctoral students to emeritus professors. A data-use and sharing agreement lets new members join and contribute to the shared database.

title: About the Project
section: Our current study and data collection effort
text:
Our current study and data collection effort
The current study applies these instruments to health and human service PONs (with plans to expand to environmental PONs) in four countries: the United States, Mexico, the Netherlands, and Spain. These four were chosen for the variation they offer in two contextual dimensions that theory suggests should matter: (i) how a country provides social welfare, and (ii) whether its policymaking runs along corporatist or pluralist lines.
The study asks two questions.

What country and municipal conditions shape how PONs are configured?
Their size, the diversity of their membership, how they are governed, and what activities they pursue. Most PON research treats networks as closed systems, bracketing the environment they operate in. Drawing on historical institutionalism and population ecology, this aim asks what the environment actually does.


Which configurations are associated with network functioning and performance?
Our focus here is not on which single factor matters most, but which combinations work, since resources, governance, size, composition, and theory of change plausibly operate in concert rather than independently.
This framing drives our analytic approach. The project uses qualitative comparative analysis, a set-theoretic method that asks which combinations of conditions are associated with an outcome, rather than estimating the average independent effect of each. QCA accommodates an intermediate number of cases, treats each network as a whole configuration rather than a bundle of separable variables, and allows for equifinality (i.e., more than one pathway to the same result).

title: About the Project
text:
Why this work matters
The result will be a first-of-its-kind comparative database on PONs that includes qualitative, quantitative, and social network data at organizational, network, municipal, and country levels.
The instruments are open, the protocols are documented, and the sharing agreement will be designed so that other scholars can collect comparable data on PONs in contexts we have not studied. The aim develop an infrastructure and database that outlasts any single paper, so that the field can more effectively test important relationships and guide effective management of these systems.
